title: Diabetes Screening in Early Childhood
author: John Wills Lloyd
summary: A short research note that takes a JAMA screening study and extends it to special education practice. Lloyd summarises Winkler and colleagues' German findings, that roughly three hundredths of one percent of children screened had presymptomatic type 1 diabetes, that nearly ten percent of those went on to clinical disease, and that the screening procedures caught more than eighty percent of cases. His own contribution is the inference the authors did not draw: because children with autism, Down syndrome or intellectual disability carry elevated diabetes risk, a screening protocol of this kind has disproportionate value for that population. He argues the practical consequence in two steps, that identified children could be monitored on a schedule for onset and could become candidates for early and ideally preventative intervention. The closing move is the one that makes the note useful to educators, a direct concession that diabetes is not an educational issue paired with a claim that student well-being still obliges special educators to tell parents screening exists. It is brief by design and reads as a pointer to the underlying study with four supporting citations.
points: The study's own numbers are modest in prevalence but high in detection, with screening identifying over eighty percent of presymptomatic cases.
Lloyd's move is to connect a finding that did not examine disability to four literatures showing elevated diabetes risk in autism, Down syndrome and intellectual disability.
He frames the practical payoff as scheduled reassessment for monitoring onset rather than a single screening event.
The note concedes that diabetes is not an educational issue and grounds the recommendation in student well-being instead.
quotes: Publishing in the Journal of the American Medical Association, Christiane Winkler and. colleagues reported that about 0.03% of children in their German sample had presymptomatic type 1 diabetes and that nearly 10% of those children later developed clinical type 1 diabetes.
They found that their screening procedures identified over 80% of those cases.

Although the researchers did not directly examine it, I thought this finding was of special interest, because children with disabilities—including autism, Down syndrome, or intellectual disability (Dhanasekara et al., 2023; Lagan et al., 2020; Wallén et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2025)—are at higher risk for developing diabetes.
Those who are at risk for developing type 1 diabetes could be reassessed regularly to monitor for the onset of diabetes.
And, they could be candidates for early—and we would hope, preventative— intervention.
Parents of children with disabilities will, I hope, request screening.
Even though diabetes may not be an educational issue, in consideration of students’ general well-being, educators of children with disabilities should alert parents to the value of screening.
